title: Truth's letters
hook: alef, mem, tav: some teachers say remove the alef and it becomes met, dead

segments.voice: Yesterday, A-M-N: emunah, amen, and the craftsman whose work holds. Your line was faith is steadiness. Did an amen land any differently? Day one thousand three hundred sixty-three.

What's the distance between true and dead? In Hebrew, one letter. The word for truth is emet, spelled alef, mem, tav. Put your thumb over the alef and two letters are left: mem, tav. Read them and you get met. Dead. Some teachers have built a whole lesson on that missing letter. A later legend even turns it into a story: a clay figure, a golem, comes alive when emet is written on its forehead, and stops when someone erases the alef. That's a legend, told and retold, not scripture. But the question it points at is a real one, and it's today's word.
screen: `EMET: ALEF, MEM, TAV.` → `COVER THE ALEF: MET.` → `A LEGEND, NOT SCRIPTURE.`

segments.voice: Emet. Truth. Four ways into it. First, the spelling. Alef opens the alef-bet. Tav closes it. Mem stands near the middle. The Talmud, in tractate Shabbat, says the seal of the Holy One is emet, and some readers notice that the word reaches from the first letter, through the center, to the last. Truth, on that reading, isn't one corner of the picture. It runs from beginning to end. Second, the alef. It makes no sound of its own. You can read the word out loud and barely notice it's there. Some teachers read that silent first letter as a sign of the One, God, at the head of every true thing. Take it away and what's left is met. The lesson they draw: words can be accurate and still lifeless, if the first thing is missing. Third, the text. The prophet Zechariah says: "Speak ye every man the truth to his neighbour." To his neighbor. Truth here is something said to someone, face to face. And a psalm says: "The LORD is nigh unto all them that call upon him, to all that call upon him in truth." In truth there means more than correct facts. It means meaning what you say. Fourth, an ordinary Tuesday. Plenty of dead truths aren't lies. They're facts with the alef taken off: correct and cold, or correct and missing the part that would change the picture. Keep the first letter, the teachers say, and the words stay alive.
screen: `FIRST, MIDDLE, LAST LETTER.` · `THE SILENT ALEF.` · `SPEAK TRUTH TO YOUR NEIGHBOR.` · `ACCURATE IS NOT ENOUGH.` · then, large: `TRUTH NEEDS THE ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep the first letter in your truth. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something true you need to say to someone soon. Maybe hard news, maybe a correction, maybe just how a thing went. Say it to yourself the way it first comes out. Then ask: is the alef there? Is the care there, the reason it matters, the part you'd rather leave out? Shape it again, one sentence, with nothing false added and nothing living taken away. Then just breathe with it. If you pray, you can bring that sentence with you when you pray. The bell holds the time.
Emet. Truth: alef, mem, tav, from the first letter to the last. Without its alef, it reads met. Today's word.
Your line: truth needs the one. Today, before you say one true thing that matters, check for the alef: is it accurate, and is it alive? Day one thousand three hundred sixty-three.

howItsDone: Jewish teachers cite the Talmud's line that God's seal is truth, and the closing words of the Shema in the prayer book run straight into the word emet.

fork.setup: a friend asks what you thought of the speech they just gave. it ran long, and one story in it was beautiful. what do you say?
options: "the story about your father was beautiful. it ran long around it."
fork.reveal: on the teachers' reading, the first answer is accurate but missing its alef, and the second isn't true at all. the third keeps both the facts and the care.

original.note: Hebrew: truth; spelled alef, mem, tav. Without the alef, מֵת, met, dead.

notes: Shabbat 55a paraphrased ('the seal of the Holy One is emet'); the first-middle-last letter explanation is attributed there to Resh Lakish in some versions and appears in the Jerusalem Talmud (Sanhedrin 1:1). Script says only 'some readers notice'. Confirm.
Mem is described as 'near the middle' of the alef-bet; confirm phrasing.
The emet/met teaching and the golem legend are labeled as teachers' reading and later legend. Confirm the golem mention is appropriate for this path.
Alef read as 'a sign of the One' (outline's 'truth needs the one') is given as some teachers' reading; the numeric value of alef is left out under the claims rule.
howItsDone: the Shema's closing 'the LORD your God' is joined to 'emet' in the liturgy; confirm wording.
